content: Mefloquine is a medication prescribed to treat and prevent malaria, a potentially fatal disease transmitted by mosquitoes in certain regions. It belongs to a class of drugs known as antimalarials and works by killing the organisms responsible for malaria. Mefloquine is available in tablet form and is taken orally. For malaria prevention, it is typically taken once a week on the same day each week. Treatment should begin 1 to 3 weeks before traveling to a malaria-endemic area and continue for 4 weeks after leaving the area. When used to treat malaria, the dosing schedule will be determined by your doctor. Always take mefloquine with food, preferably your main meal, and at least 8 ounces of water. For children, smaller and more frequent doses may be recommended. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not alter the dosage or frequency without medical advice. The tablets can be swallowed whole or crushed and mixed with a liquid such as water, milk, or sugar water. If you vomit within 30 minutes of taking the medication, take another full dose. If vomiting occurs 30 to 60 minutes after taking the medication, take another half dose. If vomiting persists after taking the additional dose, contact your doctor. Mefloquine may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking mefloquine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to mefloquine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, quinidine, quinine, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Certain medications, such as anticoagulants, antidepressants, antihistamines, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, and medications for diabetes, mental illness, seizures, or irregular heartbeat, may interact with mefloquine. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, psychosis, or schizophrenia, as well as seizures, or liver, heart, or eye disease. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, use birth control while taking mefloquine and for 3 months after stopping the medication. If you become pregnant while taking mefloquine, contact your doctor. Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking this medication. Mefloquine may cause drowsiness or dizziness, which can persist after stopping the medication. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how the medication affects you. While mefloquine reduces the risk of malaria, it does not guarantee complete protection. Continue to take precautions against mosquito bites, such as wearing long sleeves and pants, using insect repellent, and sleeping under a bed net. Plan ahead in case you experience serious side effects and need to stop taking mefloquine, especially if you are in a remote area without access to medical care. You may need an alternative medication to prevent malaria or leave the malaria-endemic area. If you are taking mefloquine to treat malaria, your symptoms should improve within 48 to 72 hours after completing treatment. Contact your doctor if your symptoms do not improve. Avoid vaccinations without consulting your doctor, as they may need to be completed before starting mefloquine. Long-term use of mefloquine may cause liver or eye damage, so your doctor may recommend periodic eye and liver function tests. Continue your normal diet unless otherwise instructed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Mefloquine may cause side effects. Common side effects include upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, loss of appetite, muscle pain, dizziness, loss of balance, ringing in the ears, headache, drowsiness, difficulty sleeping, and unusual dreams. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include tingling in the fingers or toes, difficulty walking, seizures, uncontrollable shaking, extreme nervousness or worry, depression, mood changes, panic attacks, forgetfulness, confusion, hallucinations, violent behavior, paranoia, suicidal thoughts, or rash. Some side effects may persist after stopping the medication. Report any unusual symptoms to your doctor. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store mefloquine in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call emergency services at 911 if the individual has collapsed or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, dizziness, loss of balance, headache, drowsiness, difficulty sleeping, unusual dreams, tingling in the fingers or toes, difficulty walking, seizures, or changes in mental health. Keep all medical and laboratory appointments while taking mefloquine. Your doctor may order tests and eye exams to monitor your response to the medication. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Mefloquine is sold under the brand name Lariam®.
